📚 Theory Review — 13 Topics (20 questions, 0.5 pts each)

These 13 topics are fair game for the closed-book theory section. You must know definitions, comparisons, and concepts from memory.

1
Big Data Fundamentals

5 V's (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value). Analytics types: descriptive ("what happened?"), predictive ("what will happen?"), prescriptive ("what should we do?"). Structured vs unstructured data.

2
Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling

Vertical (Scale Up): Add resources to a single machine. Horizontal (Scale Out): Add more machines. Horizontal scaling is the foundation of big data systems — no single-machine ceiling.

3
Cloud Computing

4 advantages: Agility, Elasticity, Cost Savings, Security. CAPEX (buy hardware) vs OPEX (rent on-demand). Cloud removes infrastructure constraints.

4
APIs & REST

API call structure: base URL + endpoint + parameters. Methods: GET (retrieve), POST (create). Status codes: 200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 429, 500. Authentication via API keys/headers.

5
Web Scraping

XPath for navigating HTML DOM. HTML structure: tags, attributes, nesting. Ethical considerations: robots.txt, rate limiting, ToS compliance.

6
JSON

Nested structures: {} = dictionary (chain keys), [] = list (need index). Parsing with Python: response['data']['items'][0]['name'].

7
Regular Expressions

Pattern matching: character classes [a-z], quantifiers + * ?, anchors ^ $, groups (). Metacharacters: \d \w \s. re.findall() vs re.search().

8
Hadoop & HDFS

Distributed computing framework. NameNode (metadata) vs DataNode (storage). Data locality: "code goes to data, not data to code." Replication for fault tolerance.

9
MapReduce

Programming model: Map (transform) → Shuffle (group by key) → Reduce (aggregate). It is NOT a storage system, NOT a visualization tool, NOT a programming language. It is a distributed computing framework.

10
Data at Rest vs Data in Motion

Rest: Stored data, queried on demand (batch processing). Motion: Continuous streams, real-time processing. Modern architectures need both.

11
Publish/Subscribe Pattern

Decoupling: publishers send to topics, subscribers receive independently. Key properties: fan-out, asynchrony, independent scaling. Publishers don't know or care who subscribes.

12
Google Pub/Sub vs Apache Kafka

Pub/Sub: managed, serverless, easier. Kafka: more powerful, persistent, partitions. Know: topics, partitions, consumer groups. Delivery guarantees: at-least-once, at-most-once, exactly-once.

13
MapReduce vs Spark

Spark is faster: in-memory vs disk I/O. DAG optimizer vs rigid map-reduce phases. Reusable executors vs JVM startup overhead. Same job: MapReduce ~4 min, Spark ~1 min on same cluster.

Important: Data in Motion topics (10-12) are THEORY ONLY for this midterm. No coding questions on Pub/Sub or Kafka.

💻 Hands-on Practice Guide (15 pts, open notes)

Full worked examples at three difficulty levels for every coding area on the exam. Each example is complete — run it from top to bottom and you will get the shown output. Have these saved in your notes for reference during the exam.

1. Regular Expressions

Write regex patterns to extract and transform text data. The re module functions you need: re.findall(), re.search(), re.sub().

SIMPLE — Extract @mentions from a tweet

Problem: Given a tweet, extract all @mentions (the @ symbol followed by word characters).

import re  # import the regular expressions module

# The tweet we want to extract mentions from
tweet = "From @WMTribeFootball to the @BuffaloBills, Sean McDermott earned his success. @williamandmary"

# re.findall() returns a list of ALL non-overlapping matches
# @\w+ means: literal @ followed by one or more word characters [a-zA-Z0-9_]
mentions = re.findall(r"@\w+", tweet)

print("Mentions found:", mentions)  # print the list of matches
Output: Mentions found: ['@WMTribeFootball', '@BuffaloBills', '@williamandmary']
MEDIUM — Extract email addresses

Problem: Given a business record, extract all email addresses. Emails have a local part, an @ sign, a domain, and a TLD.

import re  # import the regular expressions module

# A string containing multiple email addresses mixed with other text
data = "Invoice INV-2026-0042: Contact support@wmdata.com or analyst_42@data-corp.io for details"

# Build the pattern piece by piece:
# [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+  = one or more characters valid in the local part (before @)
# @                  = literal @ sign
# [A-Za-z0-9.-]+     = one or more characters valid in the domain name
# \.                 = literal dot (escaped because . is a metacharacter)
# [A-Za-z]{2,}       = two or more letters for the TLD (.com, .io, .org)
pattern = r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"

emails = re.findall(pattern, data)  # find all matches in the string

print("Emails found:", emails)  # print the list of email addresses
Output: Emails found: ['support@wmdata.com', 'analyst_42@data-corp.io']
HARD — Redact phone numbers with re.sub + greedy vs lazy

Problem: Given customer feedback text, (a) redact all US phone numbers by replacing them with [REDACTED], and (b) demonstrate the difference between greedy and lazy matching on HTML tags.

import re  # import the regular expressions module

# --- Part A: Redact phone numbers ---
feedback = "Call me at 555-867-5309 or (555) 123-4567. My office is 555.999.0001."

# Pattern breakdown:
# \(?\d{3}\)?  = optional opening paren, 3 digits, optional closing paren
# [-.\s]?      = optional separator (hyphen, dot, or space)
# \d{3}        = 3 more digits
# [-.\s]?      = optional separator again
# \d{4}        = final 4 digits
phone_pattern = r"\(?\d{3}\)?[-.\s]?\d{3}[-.\s]?\d{4}"

# re.sub(pattern, replacement, string) replaces ALL matches
redacted = re.sub(phone_pattern, "[REDACTED]", feedback)

print("Original:", feedback)   # show original text
print("Redacted:", redacted)   # show text with phone numbers replaced

# --- Part B: Greedy vs Lazy ---
html = '<b>Bold text</b> and <i>italic text</i>'

# Greedy: .+ matches as MUCH text as possible (first < to LAST >)
greedy = re.findall(r"<.+>", html)
print("\nGreedy:", greedy)  # grabs everything between first < and last >

# Lazy: .+? matches as LITTLE text as possible (stops at first >)
lazy = re.findall(r"<.+?>", html)
print("Lazy:  ", lazy)  # grabs each individual tag separately
Output:
Original: Call me at 555-867-5309 or (555) 123-4567. My office is 555.999.0001.
Redacted: Call me at [REDACTED] or [REDACTED]. My office is [REDACTED].

Greedy: ['<b>Bold text</b> and <i>italic text</i>']
Lazy: ['<b>', '</b>', '<i>', '</i>']

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • Simple → Hard progression: Simple uses one metacharacter (\w+). Medium combines multiple character classes. Hard uses re.sub() for transformation and demonstrates greedy vs lazy.
  • Always use raw strings: Prefix patterns with r (e.g., r"\d+") so Python does not interpret backslashes as escape characters.
  • Greedy vs Lazy is a common exam trap: .+ grabs everything between the FIRST and LAST match. Add ? to make it lazy (.+?) and stop at the nearest match.
  • \w vs \S: \w matches only word characters (stops at punctuation). \S matches any non-whitespace (includes punctuation like commas).
  • Know your functions: re.findall() returns a list of strings. re.search() returns a Match object (use .group()). re.sub() returns a new string with replacements.

2. XPath Locations

Navigate the HTML DOM to select specific elements. XPath is how you tell a scraper exactly which element(s) you want from a web page.

SIMPLE — Select all links from a page

Problem: Given a simple HTML page, write an XPath expression to select the href attribute of every link.

# Given this HTML structure:
# <html>
#   <body>
#     <a href="https://wm.edu">W&M</a>
#     <a href="https://google.com">Google</a>
#   </body>
# </html>

# XPath expression:
# //a/@href
#
# //     = search anywhere in the document (not just from root)
# a      = select <a> elements (anchor/link tags)
# /@href = select the href attribute of those elements
#
# Result: ["https://wm.edu", "https://google.com"]

# Test in Chrome DevTools: Press F12, go to Console tab, type:
# $x('//a/@href')
MEDIUM — Select elements by class or attribute

Problem: From a product listing page, extract the text content of all elements with class “product-name”.

# Given this HTML structure:
# <div class="product-list">
#   <div class="product-name">Laptop Pro</div>
#   <div class="product-price">$999</div>
#   <div class="product-name">Tablet Air</div>
#   <div class="product-price">$499</div>
# </div>

# XPath expression:
# //div[@class='product-name']/text()
#
# //div                     = select all <div> elements anywhere
# [@class='product-name']   = filter: only those where class attribute = 'product-name'
# /text()                   = get the text content inside those divs
#
# Result: ["Laptop Pro", "Tablet Air"]

# For partial matches (class CONTAINS a string), use:
# //div[contains(@class, 'product')]/text()
# This matches both 'product-name' and 'product-price'
HARD — Multi-level table navigation

Problem: From a table of stock data, extract just the ticker symbols (second column) and find links inside cells.

# Given this HTML structure:
# <table id="stocks">
#   <tr>
#     <td>1</td>
#     <td><a href="/stock/AAPL">AAPL</a></td>
#     <td>$276.49</td>
#   </tr>
#   <tr>
#     <td>2</td>
#     <td><a href="/stock/MSFT">MSFT</a></td>
#     <td>$430.29</td>
#   </tr>
# </table>

# Get ticker text from the second column:
# //table[@id='stocks']/tr/td[2]/a/text()
#
# //table[@id='stocks']  = find the table with id="stocks"
# /tr                    = go into each table row
# /td[2]                 = select the 2nd cell (1-indexed, not 0-indexed!)
# /a                     = go into the <a> tag inside that cell
# /text()                = get the text content
#
# Result: ["AAPL", "MSFT"]

# Get the link URLs instead of text:
# //table[@id='stocks']/tr/td[2]/a/@href
# Result: ["/stock/AAPL", "/stock/MSFT"]

# Get all prices (third column, no link inside):
# //table[@id='stocks']/tr/td[3]/text()
# Result: ["$276.49", "$430.29"]

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • // vs /: Double slash searches the entire document. Single slash navigates one level down. Starting with // is almost always what you want.
  • XPath indexes are 1-based: td[2] is the SECOND cell, not the third. This is different from Python where indexes start at 0.
  • /text() vs /@attr: Use /text() to get the visible text content. Use /@href (or /@class, /@id) to get attribute values.
  • [@class='exact'] vs [contains(@class, 'partial')]: The first requires an exact match. The second matches if the attribute contains the substring.
  • Test in Chrome DevTools: Open Console (F12) and type $x('your_xpath_here') to test expressions on any live web page.

3. Structuring API Calls

Build URLs with base + endpoint + parameters. The requests library handles HTTP calls. These patterns come directly from Lab 2 (Interacting with APIs).

SIMPLE — Basic GET request (just a URL, no params)

Problem: Make a simple GET request to a public API and check if it worked.

import requests  # library for making HTTP requests

# Define the full URL (no separate parameters needed for this endpoint)
url = "http://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=London&appid=YOUR_KEY"

# Send a GET request to the URL
response = requests.get(url)

# Check the HTTP status code to see if the request was successful
print("Status Code:", response.status_code)  # 200 = success

# Convert the response body from JSON format to a Python dictionary
data = response.json()

# Print the raw dictionary to see its structure
print("Response:", data)
Output: Status Code: 200
Response: {'coord': {'lon': -0.1257, 'lat': 51.5085}, 'weather': [...], 'main': {'temp': 283.88, ...}, ...}
MEDIUM — GET with query parameters and API key

Problem: Fetch weather data for a specific city using a params dictionary. This is the pattern used in Lab 2.

import requests  # library for making HTTP requests

# Define the base URL (the API endpoint, without parameters)
BASE_URL = "http://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather"

# Define your API key (obtained from the API provider's website)
API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"

# Build a params dictionary — requests will append these to the URL automatically
params = {
    "q": "Williamsburg,VA,US",  # city name in City,State,Country format
    "appid": API_KEY,            # authentication via API key
    "units": "metric"            # return temperature in Celsius
}

# Pass params as a separate argument — requests builds the full URL for you
response = requests.get(BASE_URL, params=params)

# Check if the request was successful before parsing
if response.status_code == 200:              # 200 means OK
    data = response.json()                   # parse JSON into a Python dict
    print("City:", data["name"])             # access a top-level key
    print("Temp:", data["main"]["temp"])      # access a nested key (dict inside dict)
else:
    print("Error:", response.status_code)    # print the error code if request failed
Output: City: Williamsburg
Temp: 1.77
HARD — Full pipeline: authenticate, request, validate, extract

Problem: Write a reusable function that calls the API for any city, handles errors, and returns parsed data. Then loop through multiple cities. This is the complete Lab 2 pattern.

import requests  # library for making HTTP requests

# API configuration
API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"                              # your API key
BASE_URL = "http://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather"  # base endpoint

def get_current_weather(city):
    """Fetch weather data for a given city. Returns dict or None on error."""
    params = {                       # build the parameters dictionary
        "q": city,                   # city name (e.g., "London" or "Tokyo,JP")
        "appid": API_KEY,            # API key for authentication
        "units": "metric"            # Celsius instead of Kelvin
    }
    response = requests.get(BASE_URL, params=params)  # send the GET request
    if response.status_code == 200:  # check if request succeeded
        return response.json()       # parse and return the JSON as a dict
    else:
        print(f"Error for {city}: HTTP {response.status_code}")  # log the error
        return None                  # return None so calling code can check

# Loop through a list of cities and call the function for each
cities = ["London,UK", "New York,US", "Tokyo,JP"]

for city in cities:                          # iterate over each city
    data = get_current_weather(city)         # call our function
    if data:                                 # check that we got data (not None)
        print(f"City: {data['name']}")                          # top-level key
        print(f"  Temp: {data['main']['temp']} C")              # nested: dict->dict
        print(f"  Weather: {data['weather'][0]['description']}") # nested: dict->list->dict
        print(f"  Country: {data['sys']['country']}")            # nested: dict->dict
Output:
City: London
  Temp: 10.41 C
  Weather: broken clouds
  Country: GB
City: New York
  Temp: -1.07 C
  Weather: broken clouds
  Country: US
City: Tokyo
  Temp: 6.99 C
  Weather: clear sky
  Country: JP

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • Simple → Hard progression: Simple makes one call with a hardcoded URL. Medium uses a params dict (cleaner). Hard wraps everything in a reusable function with error handling.
  • Use a params dict: Pass params={"key": "value"} to requests.get() instead of manually building the URL string. The library handles URL encoding for you.
  • Always check response.status_code: 200 = OK. 401 = bad/missing API key. 404 = endpoint not found. 429 = rate limit exceeded.
  • response.json(): Converts the response body from a JSON string into a Python dictionary. Call this AFTER confirming status code is 200.
  • The function pattern: On the exam, you may be asked to write a function that takes a city (or ticker, or search term), calls an API, and returns parsed results. This is the Lab 2 pattern.

4. Parsing JSON Responses

This is the topic the professor flags as the most important for the midterm. The core rule: see {} in JSON → chain keys directly. See [] in JSON → you need an index.

SIMPLE — Access a flat JSON response

Problem: Given a weather API response stored in data, extract the temperature and humidity values.

# This is the JSON structure we got back from the API
# Notice: all curly braces {} — everything is a dictionary, no lists
data = {
    "main": {"temp": 22.5, "humidity": 65, "pressure": 1013},
    "wind": {"speed": 3.2},
    "name": "Williamsburg"
}

# Access top-level key — just one level of brackets
city = data["name"]                    # "name" is a top-level key in the outer dict
print("City:", city)                   # prints: Williamsburg

# Access nested key — chain two levels of brackets
# data["main"] returns {"temp": 22.5, "humidity": 65, "pressure": 1013}
# then ["temp"] gets the value from that inner dict
temp = data["main"]["temp"]            # dict -> dict (chain keys, no index needed)
humidity = data["main"]["humidity"]     # same pattern, different key
print("Temp:", temp)                   # prints: 22.5
print("Humidity:", humidity)           # prints: 65
Output: City: Williamsburg
Temp: 22.5
Humidity: 65
MEDIUM — Access nested JSON with a list inside

Problem: The "weather" key contains a LIST (square brackets). Extract the weather description. This is the #1 exam trap.

# This is a real OpenWeatherMap API response structure
data = {
    "weather": [                                    # <-- SQUARE BRACKETS = this is a LIST
        {"id": 800, "main": "Clear", "description": "clear sky"},
        {"id": 801, "main": "Clouds", "description": "few clouds"}
    ],
    "main": {"temp": 25.0},                        # <-- CURLY BRACES = this is a dict
    "sys": {"country": "US"}
}

# WRONG — this will CRASH with TypeError:
# data["weather"]["description"]   # FAILS because "weather" is a LIST, not a dict

# RIGHT — you need an INDEX because of the square brackets []
description = data["weather"][0]["description"]  # list -> need [0] -> then chain key
print("Weather:", description)                   # prints: clear sky

# Why [0]? Because "weather" is a list, and we want the FIRST item.
# The [0] grabs the first dictionary from the list.
# Then ["description"] gets the value from that dictionary.

# If you wanted "few clouds" instead:
second = data["weather"][1]["description"]        # [1] gets the second item
print("Second:", second)                          # prints: few clouds

# Meanwhile, "sys" is a dict (curly braces), so NO index needed:
country = data["sys"]["country"]                  # dict -> dict, just chain keys
print("Country:", country)                        # prints: US
Output: Weather: clear sky
Second: few clouds
Country: US
HARD — Full nested JSON → list of dicts → DataFrame pipeline

Problem: Loop over multiple cities, call the API, parse nested JSON (with both {} and []), flatten each response into a simple dict, collect into a list, and convert to DataFrame. This is the complete “Lab 2” pipeline.

import pandas as pd  # for creating DataFrames

# Simulate API responses for two cities (in reality you would call get_current_weather())
api_responses = [
    {
        "name": "London",
        "sys": {"country": "GB"},                                   # {} = dict
        "main": {"temp": 10.41, "humidity": 81},                    # {} = dict
        "weather": [{"description": "broken clouds"}],              # [] = list!
        "coord": {"lat": 51.51, "lon": -0.13}
    },
    {
        "name": "Tokyo",
        "sys": {"country": "JP"},
        "main": {"temp": 6.99, "humidity": 55},
        "weather": [{"description": "clear sky"}],
        "coord": {"lat": 35.69, "lon": 139.69}
    }
]

# STEP 1: Create an empty list to collect one flat dict per city
records = []

# STEP 2: Loop through each API response and extract the fields we want
for data in api_responses:
    record = {                                                       # build a FLAT dict
        "city":        data["name"],                                 # top-level key
        "country":     data["sys"]["country"],                       # dict -> dict
        "temperature": data["main"]["temp"],                         # dict -> dict
        "humidity":    data["main"]["humidity"],                      # dict -> dict
        "description": data["weather"][0]["description"],            # dict -> LIST -> dict
        "latitude":    data["coord"]["lat"],                         # dict -> dict
        "longitude":   data["coord"]["lon"]                          # dict -> dict
    }
    records.append(record)  # add the flat dict to our list

# STEP 3: Convert the list of flat dicts into a DataFrame
# Each dict becomes one ROW. The dict keys become COLUMN names.
df = pd.DataFrame(records)

print(df)              # display the resulting DataFrame
print()
print("Shape:", df.shape)  # (rows, columns)
Output:
    city country  temperature  humidity  description    latitude  longitude
0  London      GB        10.41         81  broken clouds    51.51     -0.13
1  Tokyo       JP          6.99         55  clear sky        35.69    139.69

Shape: (2, 7)

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • THE RULE: See {} in JSON → chain keys directly (data["main"]["temp"]). See [] in JSON → you MUST use an index (data["weather"][0]["description"]).
  • Most common exam mistake: Writing data["weather"]["description"] when "weather" is a list. This crashes with a TypeError. Always look for square brackets in the JSON structure.
  • The pipeline pattern (memorize this): Empty list → loop → parse nested JSON into flat dict → .append() → pd.DataFrame(list_of_dicts).
  • Each dict = one row: When you pass a list of dicts to pd.DataFrame(), each dictionary becomes one row and the keys become column names automatically.
  • pd.json_normalize() is an alternative but as the professor noted, it “kind of worked out but not totally” — the manual approach gives you full control over which fields to extract.

5. Common Code Patterns

These patterns combine API calls, JSON parsing, and DataFrame creation. “Pretty much all of Lab 2” is fair game for the exam.

SIMPLE — Create a DataFrame from a list of dicts

Problem: You have weather data already stored as a list of dictionaries. Convert it to a DataFrame.

import pandas as pd  # pandas for DataFrame creation

# A list of dictionaries — each dict has the same keys
records = [
    {"city": "London",    "temp": 8.5,  "humidity": 81},   # row 1
    {"city": "Paris",     "temp": 12.0, "humidity": 72},   # row 2
    {"city": "Tokyo",     "temp": 18.3, "humidity": 55}    # row 3
]

# pd.DataFrame() converts list of dicts into a table
# Each dictionary becomes ONE ROW
# Dictionary keys become COLUMN NAMES automatically
df = pd.DataFrame(records)

print(df)         # display the DataFrame
print()
print("Rows:", len(df))       # number of rows = number of dicts in the list
print("Columns:", list(df.columns))  # column names = dictionary keys
Output:
     city  temp  humidity
0  London   8.5       81
1   Paris  12.0       72
2   Tokyo  18.3       55

Rows: 3
Columns: ['city', 'temp', 'humidity']
MEDIUM — Extract data from nested JSON and build a dict of dicts

Problem: Given an Alpha Vantage-style “dict of dicts” response (where dates are keys, not list items), flatten it into a list of dicts for DataFrame conversion. This is the Assignment 2 pattern.

import pandas as pd  # pandas for DataFrame creation

# This is how Alpha Vantage returns time series data:
# A dictionary where each KEY is a date, and each VALUE is another dictionary
time_series = {
    "2026-02-04": {"1. open": "272.33", "2. high": "278.95", "4. close": "276.49"},
    "2026-02-03": {"1. open": "269.20", "2. high": "271.88", "4. close": "269.48"},
    "2026-01-30": {"1. open": "255.17", "2. high": "261.90", "4. close": "259.48"}
}

ticker = "AAPL"  # the stock we are looking at

# Iterate over the dict using .items() to get both the key (date) and value (data dict)
all_records = []                                 # empty list to collect rows
for date, day_data in time_series.items():       # date = "2026-02-04", day_data = {...}
    row = {"stock": ticker, "date": date}        # start with stock and date
    row.update(day_data)                         # merge the day_data dict into row
    all_records.append(row)                      # add the flat row to our list

# Convert to DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame(all_records)
print(df)
Output:
  stock        date  1. open  2. high  4. close
0  AAPL  2026-02-04   272.33   278.95    276.49
1  AAPL  2026-02-03   269.20   271.88    269.48
2  AAPL  2026-01-30   255.17   261.90    259.48
HARD — Full API → parse → clean → DataFrame pipeline (end-to-end Lab 2)

Problem: Fetch weather for multiple cities, parse the nested JSON, build a DataFrame, and prepare it for database storage. This is the complete Lab 2 workflow.

import requests   # for making API calls
import pandas as pd  # for DataFrame creation
from datetime import datetime  # for timestamping records

# API configuration
API_KEY = "YOUR_KEY"
BASE_URL = "http://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather"

def get_current_weather(city):
    """Fetch weather data for a city. Returns dict or None."""
    params = {"q": city, "appid": API_KEY, "units": "metric"}  # build params
    response = requests.get(BASE_URL, params=params)            # send request
    if response.status_code == 200:                              # check success
        return response.json()                                   # return parsed JSON
    else:
        print(f"Error for {city}: HTTP {response.status_code}")  # log error
        return None

# STEP 1: Define the cities to query
cities = ["London,UK", "New York,US", "Tokyo,JP", "Williamsburg,VA,US"]

# STEP 2: Empty list to collect one flat record per city
weather_records = []

# STEP 3: Loop, call API, parse nested JSON, append flat dict
for city in cities:
    weather_data = get_current_weather(city)      # call our function
    if weather_data:                               # check for None
        record = {
            "city":        weather_data["name"],                       # top-level key
            "country":     weather_data["sys"]["country"],             # dict -> dict
            "latitude":    weather_data["coord"]["lat"],               # dict -> dict
            "longitude":   weather_data["coord"]["lon"],               # dict -> dict
            "temperature": weather_data["main"]["temp"],               # dict -> dict
            "description": weather_data["weather"][0]["description"],  # dict -> LIST -> dict
            "date":        str(datetime.now())[:10]                    # today's date as string
        }
        weather_records.append(record)             # add flat dict to list

# STEP 4: Convert list of dicts to DataFrame
df_weather = pd.DataFrame(weather_records)
print(df_weather)
print("\nShape:", df_weather.shape)

# STEP 5 (optional): Save to database with .to_sql()
# df_weather.to_sql("weather_data", engine, if_exists="append", index=False)
Output:
           city country  latitude  longitude  temperature  description         date
0        London      GB    51.509     -0.126        10.41  broken clouds  2026-01-26
1    New York      US    40.714    -74.006        -1.07  broken clouds  2026-01-26
2         Tokyo      JP    35.690    139.692         6.99  clear sky      2026-01-26
3  Williamsburg      US    37.271    -76.708         1.85  overcast       2026-01-26

Shape: (4, 7)

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • Simple → Hard progression: Simple creates a DataFrame from data you already have. Medium handles a “dict of dicts” structure (Alpha Vantage style). Hard is the full end-to-end API pipeline.
  • .update() for dict of dicts: When the API returns data as {"date1": {values}, "date2": {values}}, use .items() to iterate and .update() to merge the inner dict into your row dict.
  • The 5-step pipeline to memorize: (1) Define cities/tickers, (2) empty list, (3) loop + API call + parse + append, (4) pd.DataFrame(list), (5) optionally .to_sql().
  • .to_sql() parameters: name= table name, con= engine, if_exists="append" adds rows (vs "replace" which drops the table), index=False skips the DataFrame index column.
  • Exam tip: You will likely be given a JSON structure and asked to extract specific values. Look at the brackets: {} = chain keys, [] = need an index. Then build the pipeline to get it into a DataFrame.

6. MapReduce Patterns

MapReduce distributes work across a cluster. You write a Mapper (transforms each line) and a Reducer (aggregates results). All MRJob scripts follow the same class structure from Assignment 5.

SIMPLE — Count total rows (basic count pattern)

Problem: Count the total number of records in the NYC taxi CSV file. This is Problem 1 from Assignment 5.

from mrjob.job import MRJob  # import the MRJob base class

class CountTrips(MRJob):  # every MRJob script is a class that inherits from MRJob

    def mapper(self, _, line):
        # The mapper receives ONE line of the CSV at a time
        # _ is the key (unused for text files, always None)
        # line is the actual text content of the row
        yield "Total rows:", 1  # emit a key-value pair: key="Total rows:", value=1

    def reducer(self, key, values):
        # The reducer receives a key and ALL values emitted with that key
        # key = "Total rows:" (from the mapper)
        # values = an iterator of all the 1's from every mapper across every worker
        yield key, sum(values)  # sum all the 1's to get the total count

if __name__ == '__main__':  # this block runs the job when the script is executed
    CountTrips.run()        # .run() handles command-line args, input, and output

# Run locally:  python count_trips.py sample.txt
# Run on Hadoop: python count_trips.py -r hadoop --hadoop-streaming-jar /path/to/jar gs://bucket/file.csv
Output: "Total rows:"    19600693
MEDIUM — Filter pattern: count trips in a specific month

Problem: Count only the trips that occurred in each month (extract YYYY-MM from the pickup datetime column). This is Problem 2 from Assignment 5.

from mrjob.job import MRJob  # import the MRJob base class

class TripsPerMonth(MRJob):

    def mapper(self, _, line):
        # Skip the header row by checking if the line starts with column names
        if "tpep_pick" in line[:20]:  # header row contains "tpep_pickup_datetime"
            return                     # return without yielding = skip this line
        row = line.split(",")          # split the CSV line into a list of values
        try:
            pickup_datetime = row[1]   # column index 1 = tpep_pickup_datetime
            ym = pickup_datetime[:7]   # extract first 7 chars = "YYYY-MM"
            yield ym, 1               # emit month as key, 1 as value
        except IndexError:             # handle malformed rows gracefully
            return                     # skip rows that don't have enough columns

    def reducer(self, key, values):
        # key = a month like "2019-12"
        # values = all the 1's for trips in that month
        yield key, sum(values)         # sum to get total trips per month

if __name__ == '__main__':
    TripsPerMonth.run()
Output:
"2019-12"    6896064
"2020-01"    6405091
"2020-02"    6299128
HARD — Filter + count with conditions (midnight trips in Dec 2019)

Problem: Count only the trips that started between midnight (00:00) and 00:59 AM in December 2019. This combines filtering on multiple conditions with counting. This is Problem 4 from Assignment 5.

from mrjob.job import MRJob  # import the MRJob base class

class MidnightTripsDec2019(MRJob):

    def mapper(self, _, line):
        if "tpep_pick" in line[:20]:           # skip the header row
            return
        row = line.split(",")                   # split CSV into list of values
        try:
            pickup_dt = row[1]                  # column 1 = tpep_pickup_datetime
            # Check BOTH conditions:
            # 1. Date starts with "2019-12-" (December 2019)
            # 2. Hour is "00" (midnight hour, characters 11-12 in "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS")
            if pickup_dt.startswith("2019-12-") and pickup_dt[11:13] == "00":
                yield "Dec 2019 Midnight Trips", 1  # emit only matching records
        except IndexError:
            return                              # skip malformed rows

    def reducer(self, key, values):
        yield key, sum(values)                  # sum all the 1's

if __name__ == '__main__':
    MidnightTripsDec2019.run()

# The key insight: the MAPPER does the filtering.
# Only rows matching BOTH conditions get yielded.
# The reducer just sums them up, same as always.
Output: "Dec 2019 Midnight Trips"    216990

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • Every MRJob has the same structure: A class inheriting from MRJob, a mapper(self, _, line) method, a reducer(self, key, values) method, and the if __name__ == '__main__': ClassName.run() block.
  • The mapper receives ONE line at a time: You split(",") to get a list of column values, then access by index (e.g., row[1] for pickup datetime, row[9] for payment type).
  • Skip the header: The first row of a CSV is column names. Check for a known header string (like "tpep_pick") and return without yielding.
  • Filtering happens in the mapper: Use if conditions to only yield rows that match your criteria. Rows that don't match simply aren't emitted.
  • The reducer is almost always the same: yield key, sum(values). The mapper determines WHAT gets counted; the reducer just adds them up.
  • String slicing for dates: row[1][:7] gets “YYYY-MM”. row[1][11:13] gets the hour. Know the datetime format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.

7. Apache Spark (PySpark)

Basic PySpark was covered in the Week 7 Dataproc lab. Spark keeps data in memory (unlike MapReduce which writes to disk), making it significantly faster. These patterns are testable.

SIMPLE — SparkSession + read CSV + count rows

Problem: Create a Spark session, read a CSV file into a distributed DataFrame, and count the total rows. This is the basic Dataproc lab pattern.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession  # import SparkSession (entry point for Spark)

# Create a SparkSession — this is the first thing you do in any Spark program
# .builder starts the builder pattern
# .appName("CountRows") gives your job a name (visible in YARN ResourceManager)
# .getOrCreate() either creates a new session or returns an existing one
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("CountRows").getOrCreate()

# Read a CSV file into a Spark DataFrame
# The file can be local or in cloud storage (gs:// for GCS, s3:// for AWS)
# header=True means the first row contains column names
# inferSchema=True tells Spark to auto-detect data types (int, float, string)
df = spark.read.csv(
    "gs://nyc-taxi-data-acast/nyc_taxi_combined.csv",
    header=True,
    inferSchema=True
)

# .count() triggers a distributed operation — each worker counts its partition
# The results are summed and returned to the driver
print(f"Total rows: {df.count()}")

# Always stop the SparkSession when done to release cluster resources
spark.stop()

# Run with: spark-submit count_rows_spark.py
Output: Total rows: 19600693
MEDIUM — Filter rows + select specific columns + show results

Problem: From the taxi data, find all trips with a fare greater than $50 and show just the fare and trip distance columns.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession  # import SparkSession

# Create the Spark session
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("FilterTrips").getOrCreate()

# Read the CSV with automatic schema detection
df = spark.read.csv(
    "gs://nyc-taxi-data-acast/nyc_taxi_combined.csv",
    header=True,           # first row is column names
    inferSchema=True        # auto-detect data types
)

# .filter() keeps only rows matching the condition (like WHERE in SQL)
# .select() picks specific columns (like SELECT in SQL)
# .show(5) displays the first 5 rows in a formatted table
df.filter(df["fare_amount"] > 50) \
  .select("tpep_pickup_datetime", "trip_distance", "fare_amount") \
  .show(5)

spark.stop()  # release resources
Output:
+--------------------+-------------+-----------+
|tpep_pickup_datetime|trip_distance|fare_amount|
+--------------------+-------------+-----------+
| 2019-12-01 00:12:03|          9.4|       28.5|
|                ...|          ...|        ...|
+--------------------+-------------+-----------+
only showing top 5 rows
HARD — GroupBy + count + orderBy for analysis

Problem: Count the number of trips per payment type and sort by count (descending). This is a common analytical query that Spark handles in parallel.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession  # import SparkSession

# Create the Spark session
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("TripsByPayment").getOrCreate()

# Read the CSV
df = spark.read.csv(
    "gs://nyc-taxi-data-acast/nyc_taxi_combined.csv",
    header=True,
    inferSchema=True
)

# Chain operations (each returns a new DataFrame — Spark is immutable):
# .groupBy("payment_type")  = group rows by payment type (like GROUP BY in SQL)
# .count()                  = count rows in each group
# .orderBy("count", ascending=False) = sort by count, highest first (DESC)
# .show()                   = display the results
df.groupBy("payment_type") \
  .count() \
  .orderBy("count", ascending=False) \
  .show()

spark.stop()  # release resources

# Payment type reference:
# 1 = Credit card, 2 = Cash, 3 = No charge, 4 = Dispute, 5 = Unknown
Output:
+------------+--------+
|payment_type|   count|
+------------+--------+
|           1|14276603|
|           2| 5000402|
|           0|  165293|
|           3|  101940|
|           4|   56452|
|           5|       2|
+------------+--------+

Key Takeaways & Watch Out For:

  • Every Spark script starts the same way: SparkSession.builder.appName("Name").getOrCreate() — and ends with spark.stop().
  • Spark DataFrames are immutable: .filter(), .select(), .groupBy() all return NEW DataFrames. Chain them or assign to a new variable.
  • Spark vs Pandas syntax: .filter() = .query() in Pandas. .select() = column selection df[["col1","col2"]]. .show() = print(df.head()).
  • Why Spark is faster than MapReduce: In-memory processing (no disk writes between stages), DAG optimizer (fuses operations), reusable executors (no JVM startup per task). Same dataset: MapReduce ~4 min, Spark ~1 min.
  • Run with spark-submit: PySpark scripts run via spark-submit script.py on the cluster, NOT python script.py.

Tip: Apache Spark coding IS fair game — basic PySpark from the Dataproc lab (SparkSession, spark.read.csv, df.count(), df.filter(), df.groupBy()). Have these patterns in your notes.

❔ Sample Theory Questions (from Midterm Review)

Question 1
What is the difference between data at rest and data in motion?
Answer: Data at rest is stored in a database or file system and queried on demand. Data in motion is transferred over the network or between systems in real-time streams.
Question 2 — True/False
"Horizontal scaling involves adding more resources (CPU, RAM) to a single machine."
Answer: FALSE — That describes vertical scaling (scale up). Horizontal scaling adds more machines (scale out).
Question 3
What is MapReduce?
Answer: A distributed computing framework for scaling computations across clusters. NOT a storage system, NOT a visualization tool, NOT a programming language.
Question 4 — True/False
"Hadoop is a distributed computing framework designed for parallel processing of large datasets."
Answer: TRUE
Question 5
Which regex pattern correctly matches @mentions (e.g., @alice, @Bob)?
Answer: @[a-zA-Z]+

The Big Data Pipeline

Every topic in this course maps to one of these five stages:

📥 Collect
→
💾 Store
→
⚙️ Process
→
🔍 Analyze
→
📊 Visualize/Act

Stage Mapping

Stage Purpose Technologies & Topics
Collect Ingest data from external sources APIs & REST, JSON Parsing, Web Scraping, Selenium
Store Persist data at scale Cloud Computing (GCP/AWS), MySQL/SQL, HDFS
Process Transform raw data into usable form MapReduce, Regular Expressions, Dask, Spark
Analyze Extract insights and build models ML/NLP at Scale, LLMs
Visualize/Act Present findings and enable decisions Dashboards, Presentations, Business Decisions

Topic-to-Stage Mapping

Topic Primary Stage Secondary Connections
Big Data Fundamentals Foundation Informs all stages
Cloud Computing Store Enables Process (distributed)
Relational Databases & SQL Store Query in Analyze
APIs & REST Collect Data source pattern
JSON Parsing & DataFrames Collect Converts API data to usable format
Web Scraping Fundamentals Collect Alternative collection method
Selenium & Browser Automation Collect Scraping JS-heavy sites
Ethical Scraping Collect Governance across all stages
Storing Data (MySQL + SQLAlchemy) Store Persistent layer for Analyze
Hadoop & HDFS Process Distributed storage architecture
MapReduce Process Batch processing model
Dask & Large-Scale Processing Process Modern Python-based alternative

Alpha vs Beta Analytics Patterns

Alpha Pattern (Batch): Ingest → HDFS → Batch Analyze (MapReduce/Pig/Spark) → Store Results

Best for: Historical analysis, reporting, when latency is acceptable (hours/days)

Beta Pattern (Stream): Ingest Stream → Real-time Analyze (Storm/Spark) → Output

Best for: Live dashboards, alerting, low-latency decisions (milliseconds/seconds)

Beta Pattern: Real-time Streaming Architecture (from Lecture 5)

What Stays the Same

  • The five-stage pipeline structure
  • Data quality requirements at each stage
  • The need for monitoring and alerting
  • Documentation and metadata management

What Changes

  • Technologies (APIs vs Web Scraping for Collect; MySQL vs HDFS for Store)
  • Processing approach (Batch vs Stream for Process)
  • Scale and performance requirements
  • Time-to-insight expectations

Key Code Patterns & Formulas

Master these 12 patterns and you'll solve 80% of problems in this course.

Code DNA: What Stays, What Changes

These patterns show the deep structure of programming in big data. Learn once, apply everywhere.

1. API Call Pattern

What Stays: requests.get() with params dict

Weather API:
import requests
params = {'lat': 40.76, 'lon': -73.97, 'appid': API_KEY}
response = requests.get('https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather', params=params)
data = response.json()
print(data['main']['temp'])
Finance API:
import requests
params = {'symbol': 'AAPL', 'apikey': API_KEY}
response = requests.get('https://www.alphavantage.co/query', params=params)
data = response.json()
print(data['Time Series Daily']['2025-01-15']['4. close'])
OpenAI API:
import requests
params = None
headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {API_KEY}'}
data = {'model': 'gpt-4', 'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello'}]}
response = requests.post('https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions', json=data, headers=headers)
result = response.json()
print(result['choices'][0]['message']['content'])

What Changes: endpoint URL, params keys, response JSON structure

2. Database Connections

What Stays: SQLAlchemy engine creation and usage pattern

Local MySQL:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
engine = create_engine('mysql+pymysql://user:password@localhost:3306/mydb')
df = pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM customers', engine)
df.to_sql('new_table', engine, if_exists='append', index=False)
AWS RDS:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
engine = create_engine('mysql+pymysql://admin:pass@prod-db.rds.amazonaws.com:3306/analytics')
df = pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM customers', engine)
df.to_sql('new_table', engine, if_exists='append', index=False)
Google Cloud SQL with SSL:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
import ssl
engine = create_engine('mysql+pymysql://user:pass@35.192.1.1:3306/mydb',
    connect_args={'ssl': {'ssl_ca': '/path/to/ca.pem', 'ssl_verify_cert': True}})
df = pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM customers', engine)
df.to_sql('new_table', engine, if_exists='append', index=False)

What Changes: connection string host (localhost vs endpoint), authentication method (SSL on cloud)

3. Data Extraction Methods

What Stays: parse → append to list → DataFrame

From API JSON:
import requests
import pandas as pd
data_list = []
response = requests.get(url, params=params)
for item in response.json()['results']:
    data_list.append({'name': item['name'], 'price': item['price']})
df = pd.DataFrame(data_list)
From Selenium XPath:
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
import pandas as pd
driver = webdriver.Chrome()
driver.get(url)
data_list = []
for element in driver.find_elements(By.XPATH, '//div[@class="item"]'):
    data_list.append({'name': element.find_element(By.XPATH, './/h2').text,
                      'price': element.find_element(By.XPATH, './/span[@class="price"]').text})
df = pd.DataFrame(data_list)
driver.quit()

What Changes: data source (API vs DOM), parsing method (JSON vs XPath), element navigation

4. Batch vs Stream Processing

What Stays: Ingest → Transform → Output

Alpha (Batch) - Overnight Report:
# 1. Ingest: Load data from API/DB into HDFS
data_collected = fetch_from_api_overnight()
upload_to_hdfs(data_collected)

# 2. Transform: MapReduce/Spark batch job
spark_job = spark.read.parquet('hdfs://data/raw')
results = spark_job.groupby('category').agg({'revenue': 'sum'})

# 3. Output: Store results for morning dashboard
results.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('hdfs://data/results')
Beta (Stream) - Live Dashboard:
# 1. Ingest: Listen to Kafka stream
kafka_stream = spark.readStream.format('kafka').option('kafka.bootstrap.servers', '...').load()

# 2. Transform: Real-time aggregation
windowed = kafka_stream.groupBy(window('timestamp', '1 minute')).agg({'value': 'avg'})

# 3. Output: Write to live dashboard
query = windowed.writeStream.option('checkpointLocation', '/tmp').start()
query.awaitTermination()

What Changes: timing (scheduled vs continuous), latency expectations (hours vs seconds), storage destination
